articles.title: Jensen Huang is out at Nvidia — who is Colette Kress, his interim replacement?
articles.summary: Nvidia CFO Colette Kress is taking over as an interim replacement for longtime CEO Jensen Huang, who is embroiled in scandal.
articles.content:
The Nvidia Board of Directors
announced
on Thursday morning that the company’s co-founder and CEO of 33 years, Jensen Huang, has resigned as president, CEO, and member of the board, effective immediately.
This is a shocking twist for one of the most valuable companies in the world, which designs the chips that make the AI boom possible. Few people would have predicted this turn of events even just a week ago, as Huang has been so central to Nvidia throughout the company’s existence that he never even established a
succession plan
. But Huang has now been ousted after
reports that he had affairs
with both an alleged Chinese spy and one of his direct reports at Nvidia.
While the company conducts a more thorough search for Huang’s successor, Nvidia CFO and Executive Vice President Colette Kress has taken over as interim CEO. But beyond her name and job title, what do we know about the person who will now lead a company worth about $3.8 trillion?
According to
Nvidia’s website
, Kress has worked at the company since September 2013. Before that, she spent three years as an SVP and CFO of Cisco’s Business Technology Operations Finance organization. She also worked at Microsoft for 13 years, where she spent four years as CFO of the Server and Tools division. She holds a finance degree from the University of Arizona and an MBA from Southern Methodist University.
The California-based 59-year-old has a very limited social media presence — on
Linkedin
, she has commented some well wishes on former colleagues’ posts about their retirement. But as CFO, she’s been a regular presence on Nvidia’s earnings calls, making her a familiar figure for analysts covering the company.
According to Forbes’ list of America’s Richest Self-Made Women, Kress’ net worth is estimated to be about $1.2 billion. Her
Forbes profile
adds that she initially joined Nvidia in part because her two sons endorsed the company for its role in the video game industry, which it was best known for at the time.
“Nvidias strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years,” Kress said in a
statement
. “We will continue advancing the work that has made Nvidia a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders.”
Nvidia is slated to report its quarterly earnings on Tuesday, when we will likely hear more from Kress about her plans for the company’s immediate future.

articles.title: Norwest pushes deeper into AI with new $4B fund
articles.summary: This is the investment firm's largest fund to date.
articles.content:
Norwest
, a firm backed solely by Wells Fargo, has raised a $4 billion fund as it sets out to invest more in AI. This is the eighteenth fund for the 65-year-old multi-stage investment firm, and its largest to date.
The fund will be invested across various sectors and multiple countries, notably the United States, India, and Israel. But the big story here is AI, and Norwest’s plans to expand its investment in this area.
Norwest said Thursday it aims to capitalize on AI startups developing products and services across core industries such as consumer, healthcare, and technology. The investment firm, which has backed Plaid, Spotify, Uber, and Vuori, said it will continue to expand its investments in physical AI, voice AI, agentic cybersecurity, and aerospace.
If that sounds like a broad approach, it is intended to be, Jeff Crowe, a senior managing partner at Norwest, told TechCrunch.
“We’re taking a broad approach to AI because its impact is broad,” Crowe added, as AI is not limited by industry, geography, or application. “Just as digital transformation did, AI transformation has the potential to touch most layers of enterprise, consumer, and healthcare solutions: networking, enterprise IT and applications. Adapting to an agentic environment means applying AI broadly across products and services that solve problems.”
Crowe added that the firm is particularly excited about early-stage companies building AI-native application and infrastructure, physical AI, domain-specific models, and cybersecurity solutions.
Some of the firm’s recent investments reflect this strategy. For instance, the firm invested in Coval, which builds tools to test and evaluate AI agents, and Generalist AI, a startup that has developed AI foundation models for robots.
Since the launch of its seventeenth fund, a
$3 billion
raise that closed in 2024, the firm has made more than 87 investments.

articles.title: Cyberattack on Fireworks AI allowed hackers to access Notion customers’ chat transcripts
articles.summary: This is Fireworks' second data breach in as many months.
articles.content:
A cyberattack at Fireworks AI has exposed some of its customers’ data, the company has confirmed. Fireworks AI, a platform that developers use to access and use open AI models, said an attacker breached its cloud provider to gain access to a Fireworks development system, which allowed access to some of its customers’ data.
The company said in its
latest security advisory
that the cybercriminals took Fireworks’ customers’ billing information and some datasets. Fireworks touts tens of thousands of customers worldwide using its platform, including legal tech company Harvey and AI company Cursor.
At least one confirmed affected customer is online document editor and notetaker Notion, which said
in a disclosure
that the breach affected around 1% of its own customers.
Notion said that Fireworks alerted the company to a security incident and later confirmed that the hackers had stolen some Notion customer data. On November 3, Notion said it disconnected its systems from Fireworks, deleted the data stored in its systems, and stopped all connectivity between the two.
Notion confirmed this week that the hackers took chat transcripts of its Notion AI customers who used the “Insights” feature. The company said that the transcripts include “any input to or output from the model that was written to the chat,” but added that much of the data was unattributable and could not be determined from which customer it was obtained.
The breach at Fireworks AI shows how tech companies are reliant on other tech providers for their own offerings, and how cyberattacks can, as a result, spill over into other customers.
Fireworks said that it believes the hackers are financially motivated and that their goals are focused on selling tokens from breaching access to large language models, or LLMs. These schemes rely on selling to unauthorized third parties, who can burn through AI model usage without using their own resources.
This is the second breach affecting Fireworks in as many months, following a
security incident in October
.

articles.title: Nine Korean startups vie for a spot in Disrupt 2027’s Startup Battlefield 200 competition
articles.summary: The startups work across the deep tech sector, including healthcare, fintech, energy, semiconductors, and AI. All nine are looking to enter the U.S.
articles.content:
TechCrunch’s yearly
Startup Battlefield 200
competition sees hundreds of companies from across the world trying every year to get a chance to pitch in front of VCs and the international tech community at the
TechCrunch Disrupt
conference.
This week, nine early-stage South Korean startups pitched at
DETO 2026
, a technology conference in Seoul, to earn a spot in next year’s Startup Battlefield 200.
The startups work across the deep tech sector, including healthcare, fintech, energy, semiconductors, and AI. All nine startups are looking to enter the U.S. market as part of the broader international expansion plans.
Voinosis, which develops AI to detect changes in brain health through voice analysis, won the competition. The other eight startups are listed below in alphabetical order.
Voinosis
Voinosis
is developing an AI tool that analyzes speech patterns such as pitch, pauses, rhythm, and response times to detect changes linked to brain health. Each voice check takes less than five minutes.
The company says its technology has been tested in Greek, Japanese, and English, and its product doesn’t require separate training for each language. In a clinical study involving 146 participants, the startup claims its tech achieved 88% accuracy in screening for potential cognitive issues.
Voinosis targets hospitals, senior living facilities, insurers, and individual consumers. It also plans to link voice checks with cognitive training, assessments, and treatment provided by healthcare professionals.
The startup was founded by Grace Shin, who spent more than 25 years as an otologic surgeon. The startup is currently raising a Series A round and has already secured a South Korean pharmaceutical company as a strategic investor.
Awesome Lab
Awesome Lab
, based in Seoul, makes ThermoFlux, a heating system that uses water electrolysis and ionization to generate heat. The system can manage heat production for buildings, water supply, and industrial processes. The company says its technology can reduce energy consumption and carbon emissions.
For its international expansion, Awesome Lab is taking a different approach in each market. In the U.S., it plans to supply core OEM modules and work with boiler, water heater, and HVAC companies on product development.
Crosshub
Crosshub
helps travelers and international visitors verify their identities and set up payment methods abroad. Its platform, IDBlock, combines identity verification and payment services using self-sovereign identity (SSI) and zero-knowledge proof.
The company says its platform helps users prove their identity across borders without sharing unnecessary personal information. Crosshub is also integrating this technology with payment systems to improve access to financial services for travelers.
DeepFusion AI
DeepFusion AI
has developed a 4D radar-based imaging system with additional sensors for autonomous mobility, robotaxi, maritime surveillance, and defense applications. The system combines RF sensors with radar and lidar to detect objects, movement, or distance without a direct line of sight. All sensors are supposedly packed into a single, customizable unit.
EFLOW
EFLOW
develops special motors that can produce more torque, or rotational force, while taking up less space for use in robots, drones, satellites, and other mobility applications. The startup also develops actuators that control how robotic joints move.
Otiton Medical
Otiton Medical
makes two medical devices: One specializes in measuring body temperature, while another can capture ear canal images and analyze the eardrum. The company says its AI was trained on about 55,000 images of eardrums, and the device has received medical certification in South Korea.
Riibotics
Riibotics
says it can deploy robots into warehouses within a day. Riibotics wants to reduce deployment costs for warehouses by streamlining setup, which includes infrastructure setup, warehouse mapping, system integration through custom middleware, task programming, and safety checks.
Ternell
Ternell
, a semiconductor startup based in Ulsan, is developing a new type of memory to help AI chips use less power.
Unlike conventional two-state memory, Ternell’s T-SRAM system adds a third state for more efficient data storage. Founded in 2019 by KyungRok Kim, a former Samsung Electronics engineer, Ternell reports that tests with 28-nanometer chips showed a 33% to 102% increase in memory capacity per area, and a 55% to 71% reduction in energy needed to access data, compared with conventional
SRAM.
Testbank
Testbank
is a Korean edtech startup developing Solve, an app that converts printed study materials, such as workbooks and test-prep books, into interactive digital versions.
The startup uses AI to identify question and answer spaces in publishers’ PDF files while preserving the original layout. Solve lets you write answers directly on the page and be graded automatically.

articles.title: Who could replace Jensen Huang? A highly unscientific list of possible successors
articles.summary: Nvidia has no succession plan and a CEO in hot water, so we’ve drafted a shortlist.
articles.content:
It’s almost inconceivable that Nvidia would fire its rock star CEO. Yet here we are, on the precipice of this happening. Over at Kalshi, Jensen Huang’s odds of surviving the week are sitting at a
lowly 30%
. Even though he built one of the world’s most valuable — and, many would argue,
dangerously powerful
— companies, the tides have completely turned against him. He has confessed to an extramarital affair, but as of Wednesday afternoon it isn’t even clear who he meant: Alice Huang, the Chinese executive suspected by U.S. intelligence of spying for her country, or Kimberly Powell, an Nvidia executive who reports to him and who, five sources told The New York Times in an
explosive new report,
was also a paramour.
Even if Huang is pushed out as CEO, the board members he has made very rich are unlikely to cut him loose entirely. Barring another shoe dropping, they could keep him on as chairman, a role Nvidia doesn’t currently have. But someone still has to run the company, and there’s no apparent succession plan, which leaves us, like everyone else, to speculate while we wait to see what happens next. While Huang’s 60 direct reports undoubtedly get a closer look, consider this our own parlor game, featuring some obvious and less obvious candidates:
Lisa Su
. The AMD CEO runs Nvidia’s most credible rival and is a distant cousin of Huang. The Information
floated her name
this week, but why would she leave her job for his? Her company stands to benefit from every day that Nvidia spends distracted by an investigation, congressional briefings, and all the mini dramas that are sure to follow. Her best move might be to send a nice note and keep her current corner office.
Eric Schmidt.
He was the pick of Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management, who we
talked with
earlier this week. Schmidt could “parachute in tomorrow and do a very good job,” Sonnenfeld said, and perhaps he could. He ran Google from 2001 to 2011, chaired the National Security Commission on AI from 2018 to 2021, and now runs the rocket company Relativity Space. Chips, software, government, rockets — it’s an impressive range. Then again, Schmidt would bring a
lot
of baggage when it comes to his own
extramarital dalliances
. It’s hard to see him clearing the board for that reason.
Lip-Bu Tan
. Intel’s CEO knows chips, and right now he might welcome a very soft landing. Last month, Intel reported third-quarter revenue up 21% to $16.5 billion, then warned its fourth-quarter results would fall short of Wall Street’s forecasts. The AI boom has caused a memory-chip shortage, pushing up PC prices and cutting PC sales. That’s hurt Intel (PC chips are a big part of its business), and its stock plunged 20% in after-hours trading on the warning, having already slid more than 30% since September. A move to a company that’s eating everyone’s lunch would be a pretty amazing escape hatch.
Bret Taylor.
The former Salesforce co-CEO and OpenAI board chair now runs the AI startup Sierra, and his résumé includes a lot of the biggest brands in Silicon Valley. He co-created Google Maps, served as Facebook’s CTO, and chaired Twitter’s board through its sale to Elon Musk. He then took over as OpenAI’s board chair after the “Blip,” Sam Altman’s firing and fast return. When companies need an unflappable, likable adult in the room, they call Taylor. He probably knows nearly every customer Nvidia has, too.
Ian Buck.
If the board feels strongly about having a “builder” at the helm, they could do worse than the Nvidia VP who helped develop CUDA, the chip software that has become central to Nvidia’s dominance in AI. Analysts and former employees have floated him as a possible successor, and Kalshi traders give him a
middling shot
. He’s no household name, but the Stanford PhD seems more viable if Huang can keep that chairman title and push for a successor he can work with.
Someone else down the hall.
Andrew Bell, Nvidia’s senior vice president of hardware engineering, arrived 25 years ago as a fresh Cornell grad and has been on an upward trajectory at the company ever since. Like Buck and dozens of other executives who are presumably being scrutinized, he reports directly to Huang. Nvidia CFO Colette Kress is the insider most often named, but analysts say she isn’t necessarily a natural successor as an innovator and visionary, and Bell has the chip pedigree.
The wild card?
Lori Huang
. Nobody has floated her, but hear us out: Jensen met his wife as lab partners at Oregon State, so she has been working with him since before Nvidia existed. After graduating, she worked at Silicon Graphics as a microchip engineer (making more money than her husband, he has said), then scaled back to raise the couple’s family, and she now co-leads the family trusts. If the board wants continuity, they could do worse than a humbler Huang who is also a brainiac. There’s a reason they say that behind every great man is a great woman (and vice versa).
Whatever happens next, we’ll know soon.

URL Source: https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-hydrogen/

Published Time: 2026-11-12T18:00:00+00:00

In this article
*   [Unlocking efficiencies in multi-model workloads](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-hydrogen/#efficiencies)
*   [Scaling developer and enterprise workflows](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-hydrogen/#scaling-workflows)
*   [Adaptable speed and intelligence across thinking levels](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-hydrogen/#adaptable-speed)
*   [Fast, everyday help in the Gemini app and Search](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-hydrogen/#fast-everyday-help)
*   [Designed for safe, dependable execution for scale](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-hydrogen/#safe-dependable-execution)

Today, we’re introducing Gemini 4 Hydrogen, bringing cutting-edge intelligence to everyone — with speed and efficiency for everyday coding and agentic workflows.

While our frontier models, [Gemini 4 Carbon](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/gemini-4-carbon-now-available/) and [Gemini 4 Argon](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-argon/), excel at deep, long-horizon reasoning on your hardest problems, Hydrogen is built for rapid execution across diverse agentic workflows. With Hydrogen, we’re also bringing Gemini 4 to everyone — for all tiers of [Google AI Studio](https://aistudio.google.com/prompts/new_chat?model=gemini-4-hydrogen), the Gemini API, [Gemini for business](https://cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise), the [Gemini app](http://gemini.google.com/), [Google Search](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/search/gemini-4-hydrogen-search-upgrade), and paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in [Google Antigravity](https://antigravity.google/).

Hydrogen surpasses Argon on the [Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index](https://artificialanalysis.ai/) at its default high thinking level (51 vs. 50, and reaching 54 at its highest xhigh thinking setting), while often completing tasks faster than models in its class. Gemini 4 Hydrogen is priced flat across its entire 1 million-token context window at $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens.

## Unlocking efficiencies in multi-model workloads

In real-world software development, while teams rely on frontier models like Carbon and Argon for deep architectural judgment when designing systems or untangling subtle bugs, they still need a fast, disciplined execution model for writing code, running tests, and verifying changes. Hydrogen is built to stand on its own as a model for everyday work — or to pair with Carbon and Argon as the high-efficiency execution engine in multi-model workflows.

To help make this multi-model collaboration automatic, we’re introducing [Orchestrator in Google Antigravity](https://antigravity.google/blog/gemini-4-hydrogen-in-google-antigravity). Rather than using a single model from start to finish, Orchestrator dynamically switches between models like Carbon and Hydrogen within the same session. On [Terminal-Bench 4.0](https://www.tbench.ai/news/terminal-bench-4-0), Orchestrator reached near-Carbon task success rates while, on average, consuming 24% less quota and completing 19% faster. For workflows that require parallel agents, Carbon can act as the coordinator while Hydrogen can power worker and verifier agents to build and test changes simultaneously across isolated workspaces — helping teams ship complex projects faster without driving up token costs.

## Scaling developer and enterprise workflows

Beyond multi-model workflows, Hydrogen is a major standalone upgrade for teams migrating from Gemini 3.8 Flash. It delivers significant leaps in both speed and intelligence — finishing tasks 2.5 times faster at its high default setting while more than tripling [Terminal-Bench 4.1](https://www.tbench.ai/) scores (57% vs. 18.2%), cutting fabricated claims by more than 5x, and adapting cleanly when a tool call fails or a search returns empty. It also matches or outperforms competing models in its class across core developer and enterprise workflows:

*   **Iterative repository coding and debugging:** Hydrogen handles issue resolution, debugging, rapid iteration, and codebase Q&A with focused, surgical edits — delivering cleaner, production-ready code without rewriting unrelated files. It outperforms similar-tier models on SWE-sweep where it has to discover and repair bugs without breaking existing code. To explore large repositories efficiently, the model excels at natively batching file-read and search calls in parallel rather than inspecting files one by one; in early testing across complex graphs, SQL, and data-heavy enterprise workflows, our partners have seen Hydrogen run 2x to 2.8x faster while reducing token usage by 12% to 23%, compared to 3.8 Flash.
*   **Open-ended agentic execution:** On multi-step tasks like deep research, data analysis, and broad codebase navigation, Hydrogen ranks #5 on [Agent Arena](https://arena.ai/leaderboard/agent), arena.ai’s live benchmark. For deep domain reasoning and analysis, it leads its class on HLE-Diamond (58.8%), ranks #1 overall on [Vals Tax Agent Bench](https://www.vals.ai/benchmarks/tax_agent_bench) (52.3%), ties for #1 on the [Vals Legal Research Bench](https://www.vals.ai/benchmarks/legal_research) (55.8%), and leads its class on [AutomationBench-AA](https://artificialanalysis.ai/evaluations/automationbench-aa).

*   **Multimodal knowledge work:** Hydrogen pairs native 1 million-token input with up to 1 million output tokens to synthesize dense PDFs, spreadsheets, charts, audio, and recorded video into polished, cited reports and structured deliverables. It outperforms other models on the new [Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA)](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/multimodal-knowledge-agent-benchmark/) benchmark (53.4%) for end-to-end agentic knowledge work over complex visual files, and on [Agents’ Last Exam v1.1](https://agents-last-exam.org/leaderboard) (71.6%) for end-to-end professional workflows.
*   **Web development**: On tasks where speed matters to developers, like live UI prototyping, design-to-code iteration, and interactive app building, Hydrogen generates more functional, feature-complete layouts in fewer prompts.

## Adaptable speed and intelligence across four thinking levels

We built Gemini 4 Hydrogen for real-world usability. Hydrogen’s four thinking levels — low, medium, high (default), and a new xhigh tier — offer a wide range of options across quality, latency, and cost, scaling in a smooth, predictable progression so you only wait and pay for the reasoning depth a task requires. Across thinking levels, Hydrogen matches or outperforms some of the competing models in its class while often finishing tasks faster and using fewer output tokens.

## Fast, everyday help in the Gemini app and Search

For consumers, Gemini 4 Hydrogen makes it easier to get things done, staying on track and following instructions more closely across multi-turn conversations.

In the Gemini app, Hydrogen makes your everyday assistant even more helpful — it’s better at following your guidance, calling the right tools, and getting you to a reliable output with less back-and-forth.

*   **Ready-to-go writing, research, and everyday work:** Hydrogen sticks closely to your tone, format, and specific rules, so email drafts, study guides, rewrites, and documents come back ready to use on the first try. When you are comparing products or synthesizing dense material, it pulls together clear tables and visual breakdowns without dropping key details.
*   **Connects the dots and gets more tasks done:** Hydrogen breaks down your goal step-by-step, pulling relevant context from your uploads, Google apps like Gmail and Google Drive, and Connected Apps like Airtable and Dropbox. When you start a task in Gemini, it also more frequently calls the right tools and skills for the job, helping save you time as you check things off your to-do list.
*   **Everyday prototyping and iteration:** For exploring and testing ideas, Hydrogen generates clean, working layouts in fewer prompts, making it easy to prototype and refine interactive projects quickly, like synthesizing real-time global lightning strike data into an interactive 3D globe.

Hydrogen is significantly upgrading [Search](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/search/gemini-4-hydrogen-search-upgrade), delivering more helpful, intuitive responses for all users globally.

*   **Better understands your true intent:** With Hydrogen, you can ask your question in your natural flow of thought — even if you have multiple parts to your query, hard-to-understand typos, or highly specific requests — and Search will intelligently comprehend what you’re looking for.
*   **More visual responses:** You’ll get highly adaptive, visual, and easy-to-scan responses that are uniquely relevant to your needs, at the speed you expect from Search.
*   **Wider range of relevant links:** With Hydrogen’s advanced reasoning, we’re also upgrading our query fan-out technique in Search, connecting you to a broader range of helpful links than before, helping you find sites you previously might not have discovered.

## Designed for safe, dependable execution at scale

Gemini 4 Hydrogen brings improvements from our latest Gemini 4 safety and security stack to our broadest audience yet, combining built-in training with real-time surface safeguards to help mitigate both misalignment and misuse. Beyond foundational protections, we focused on two areas that matter most for a faster model that’s for everyday work:

*   **Safe, aligned, and secure agentic workflows:** While 3.8 Flash has strong alignment and safeguards, Hydrogen is a leap ahead. It reduces overreach in agentic tasks by up to 81% and under-service by up to 79%, and cuts misaligned actions and task shortcutting across tool-use and coding evaluations by 12x. When faced with impossible or blocked tasks, it is up to 2x less likely to bypass permission boundaries and achieves a 96.7% honesty rate on our internal agent honesty evaluation.
Building on our commitment to [reasoning transparency](https://institute.deepmind.com/essays/the-case-for-reasoning-transparency/), Hydrogen also preserves 99.9% chain-of-thought legibility with zero deceptive reasoning edits across more than 200,000 audited turns. Against indirect prompt injection attacks, Hydrogen is more than 2.3x more resilient on the Gray Swan IPI benchmark, while significantly improving robustness across tool use, computer use, and coding agents.

*   **Helpful, reliable everyday interactions:** Across our product surfaces, we tuned Hydrogen to make everyday conversations more reliable and safe. Our updated safeguards are also much more precise at distinguishing between real biosecurity risks and legitimate medical or scientific questions — keeping false refusals on HealthBench Pro under 0.4%.

For more details see the Gemini 4 Hydrogen [model card](https://storage.googleapis.com/deepmind-media/Model-Cards/Gemini-4-Hydrogen-Model-Card.pdf).

## Gemini 4 Hydrogen, available to everyone today

Starting today, Hydrogen is rolling out globally across our developer, enterprise, and consumer surfaces:

Earlier this week, we introduced [Gemini 4 Carbon](https://antigravity.google/blog/gemini-4-carbon-in-google-antigravity) alongside [`/swarm`](https://antigravity.google/docs/swarm) for tackling massive, multi-worktree engineering tasks with parallel agent teams. A common industry approach is to use a static “model router” that guesses task difficulty from your first prompt and routes the entire task to the cheapest model that is good enough to complete the task. Unfortunately, these start breaking down as agents become longer running, requiring different levels of complexity at different stages, often discovered as the task evolves.

Orchestrator takes a dynamic, bidirectional approach between Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen within the evolution of a single trajectory. For example, Carbon can start in a read-only phase to explore dependencies, resolve ambiguities, and build a concrete plan with explicit re-planning triggers. Hydrogen could then take over to write edits, update packages, and run tests. If Hydrogen hits friction, it would hand back to Carbon to inspect the state, repair the plan, and resume execution. This allows Orchestrator to reach near-Carbon task success while being faster and more quota-efficient. On Terminal-Bench 4.1, Orchestrator reached near-Carbon task success rates while, on average, consuming 24% less quota and completing 19% faster.

In the demo below, an open-source issue triage system built with the Antigravity SDK pairs multiple agents together. The Hydrogen agents handle triaging and coding to keep up with incoming issue volume, searching the codebase, asking clarifying questions, and fast UI iteration from PR comments while the Carbon agent is assigned to larger refactors, new features, and security checks.

Both devices run 8B and 16B mixture-of-experts models on about 1 GB of RAM by keeping only part of each model in memory and reading the rest from flash as it's needed.
More devices (phones, single-board computers, routers) are coming. The techniques aren't tied to one box: the 1-bit kernel needs only basic NEON, and the flash streaming works on any Linux or Android device with more model than RAM.
How it works
All of it is a patch on
llama.cpp
. The main ideas:
Kernels built for the chip.
A 1-bit lookup-table kernel, repacked 2-bit and ternary formats for the Cortex-A55, and versions of them for the A7, which has no dot-product instructions.
Less RAM per model.
Most of a small model's vocabulary is rarely used, so we drop those output rows. On the TV, a "headless" mode also stops the launcher and Google services while a model runs.
Experts paged from flash.
A mixture-of-experts model only uses a few experts per token. We keep the popular ones in RAM, read the others from flash on demand and prefetch the next layer's. This is how 8B and 16B models run on 1 GB.
Streaming for dense models
bigger than RAM, at the flash's full speed.

articles.title: Chinese frontier AI models carry the fingerprint of export-controlled GPUs
articles.content:
Title: Top Chinese Frontier AI Models Carry the Fingerprint of Export-Controlled NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs

URL Source: https://unemploymentlabs.com/checkpoint-forensics

Markdown Content:
## Executive Summary

**Our forensic analysis of publicly released AI models finds evidence that DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group have gained access to NVIDIA’s Blackwell GPUs, despite restrictions on exporting these chips to China, and are using that hardware to create their AI models.** Six models released by these companies since April 2026 contain numerical patterns matching Blackwell hardware, whereas earlier models from the same companies match NVIDIA’s older Hopper generation. The findings suggest that several leading Chinese AI developers have begun using Blackwell to train their newest models. U.S. officials and press reports had already alleged that DeepSeek and Moonshot AI were using Blackwell chips, without publishing technical evidence.

The evidence comes entirely from the models’ own published weights, rather than from leaks or insider accounts. We recover traces of the models’ initial values, and then search for the hardware configurations and initial configurations that reproduce them; for DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Kimi K3, we also confirmed the match on physical Blackwell chips. The fingerprint identifies how the weights were created and supports, without proving, the inference that Blackwell also performed the training. Specially configured AMD hardware, which is also restricted from export to China, is the only alternative we have identified; we have excluded it for DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and consider it very unlikely for the other five models. Notably, our findings provide technical evidence of access to advanced computing hardware, but do not establish where the chips were located, how access was obtained, or whether export controls were violated.

**Table 1. Hardware fingerprints in successive models from DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group**[Link ↗](https://unemploymentlabs.com/checkpoint-forensics#table-1)

| Lab | Model | Released | Chip the model was started on |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DeepSeek | DeepSeek-V3 | Dec 2024 | NVIDIA Hopper (lab disclosed H800) |
|  | DeepSeek-V4-Flash | Apr 2026 | • NVIDIA Blackwell B200/B300 |
|  | DeepSeek-V4-Pro | Apr 2026 | • NVIDIA Blackwell GB200/GB300 |
| Moonshot AI | Kimi K2 | Jul 2025 | NVIDIA Hopper (lab disclosed H800) |
|  | Kimi K2.5 | Jan 2026 | NVIDIA Hopper (lab disclosed H800) |
|  | Kimi K3 | Jul 2026 | • NVIDIA Blackwell GB200/GB300 |
|  | Kimi K3.1-Pro | Nov 2026 | • NVIDIA Blackwell GB200/GB300 |
| MiniMax | MiniMax-M2.7 | Apr 2026 | NVIDIA Hopper |
|  | MiniMax-M3 | Jun 2026 | • NVIDIA Blackwell B200/B300 |
| Ant Group | Ling-3.0-flash | Aug 2026 | NVIDIA Hopper |
|  | Ling-3.1-flash | Oct 2026 | • NVIDIA Blackwell GB200/GB300 |

_• Requires a U.S. license for export to China; none have been reported._

_A Hopper fingerprint cannot distinguish an H800 from an H100 SXM or H200; the H800 identifications above are lab disclosures, not findings of this method._

## Main Findings

1.   **Six models from four Chinese labs read as Blackwell-trained.** DeepSeek-V4-Flash and MiniMax-M3 match NVIDIA’s Blackwell-class B200 or B300 chips, which have 148 processor cores (called _streaming multiprocessors_, or SMs). DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, Kimi K3.1-Pro and Ling-3.1-flash match the GB200 or GB300 chips, also Blackwell-class, which have 152 processor cores. Kimi K3.1-Pro starts from the same seed as K3, and may be a checkpoint of K3 with further post-training.
2.   **Chinese labs started training on Blackwell relatively recently.** DeepSeek’s models read as Hopper-trained through DeepSeek-V3 (released in December 2024), and as Blackwell from DeepSeek V4 (released in April 2026). Moonshot’s models read as Hopper through Kimi K2.5 (January 2026) and as Blackwell from K3 (July 2026). One Moonshot model sits in between: Kimi K2.7-Code, posted six weeks before K3, is built on the Hopper-era weights but contains a small part that matches the B200 or B300. MiniMax’s models read as Hopper through M2.7 (April 2026) and as Blackwell from M3 (June 2026). Ant Group’s Ling-3.0-flash (August 2026) reads as Hopper, while its Ling-3.1-flash (October 2026) reads as Blackwell. The Hopper readings do not identify a specific chip: H800s, H100 SXMs and H200s share the same fingerprint.
3.   **Not every Chinese AI lab has switched to Blackwell.** The newest models we could read from Alibaba (Qwen), Zhipu (GLM), Tencent, Xiaomi and StepFun all read as Hopper-trained. Meituan says its LongCat-2.0 was trained entirely on “AI ASIC superpods,” and we found no NVIDIA fingerprint in the model weights it’s released.
4.   **The method gets known answers right.** For 24 specific models, the developer has publicly said what hardware was used. In every case, our method agrees with the public announcement. NVIDIA’s own Nemotron-3 Ultra, whose technical report names the GB200 for one phase of its training, reads as 152 SMs, the same as Kimi K3.
5.   **The matches are far stronger than chance would explain.** Even unrelated numbers can appear to match when enough combinations are tried. Across the roughly 6 trillion seed-and-layout combinations in our search, the strongest chance match would be expected to reach about 8 sigma—a measure of how far a result stands above ordinary random variation. The strongest evidence for each of the six models ranges from 49 to 1,385 sigma. Even the weakest individual test we report reaches 20 sigma.
6.   **The training runs were data-center scale.** From each model’s size and the amount of data it was trained on, we estimate that each run needed on the order of 1,500 to 3,500 Blackwell GPUs for one and a half to three months, about 12,000 across the five (Table 2), assuming each model was trained on the hardware that initialized it. These estimates are rough, and the ranges around them are wide. At roughly $70,000 per GPU—the cost implied by a Wall Street Journal report that about 36,000 Blackwell chips being installed in Malaysia for ByteDance’s use would cost more than $2.5 billion—the largest of these clusters would cost about $200 million, and the five together more than half a billion dollars. These figures cover only the final training runs; the labs’ total spending on export-controlled GPUs is likely in the billions of dollars.

**Table 2. Rough scale of each training run**[Link ↗](https://unemploymentlabs.com/checkpoint-forensics#table-2)

| Model | Blackwell GPUs, best estimate | Range |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DeepSeek-V4-Flash | 1,700 | 250–5,000 |
| DeepSeek-V4-Pro | 2,700 | 750–6,500 |
| Kimi K3 | 3,400 | 1,000–9,500 |
| MiniMax-M3 | 1,400 | 200–5,000 |
| Ling-3.1-flash | 1,400 | 400–6,500 |
| All five | 12,000 | 7,000–20,000 |

_Training tokens divided by the tokens per second we assume a Blackwell GPU sustained on a model of that shape, over the run length the release timeline suggests: about 45 days for DeepSeek-V4-Flash, 70 for DeepSeek-V4-Pro, 80 for Kimi K3, 60 for MiniMax-M3 and 100 for Ling-3.1-flash._

_We are not confident in these estimates. They rest on assumptions that the weights cannot confirm. The first is how efficiently each lab used its GPUs (often called MFU): we assume less than NVIDIA’s published benchmark rates, in line with other disclosed Blackwell training runs, and no lab has published its own figure. The second is how many tokens each model was trained on: DeepSeek’s counts are its own, and we take them on trust; the others are our estimates. The third is how long each run lasted, which no lab has stated. The fourth is that training stayed on the hardware that created the weights. The figures cover only the final training run of each model, not experiments, earlier runs or serving._

## Our investigation

A model’s _weights_, also called _parameters_, are the billions of adjustable numbers that determine how it processes information and produces answers. Training repeatedly adjusts these numbers; but before training can begin, they need initial values. In the software examined here, those values come from a pseudorandom number generation (PRNG) algorithm called Philox: Philox produces seemingly random numbers in a deterministic way. The starting input for Philox is a number called the “seed.” Given the same seed and settings, Philox produces the same numbers every time. This lets engineers repeat an experiment from the same starting point.

To fill billions of weights quickly, PyTorch, the software framework used in the development of most major AI models, divides the work that Philox does among many parallel workers on the GPU, called _threads_. (It does this through cuRAND, NVIDIA’s library for random number generation.) Each thread generates its own sequence of numbers from the seed and fills a particular set of positions. The number of threads then determines how those positions are shared out. On the NVIDIA chips examined here, a sufficiently large initialization uses the maximum of 2,048 threads for each processing unit, called a _streaming multiprocessor_ (SM). A chip with more SMs therefore assigns the same job to more workers, changing where their numbers go.

**Figure 1** illustrates how this works on a simplified GPU with six SMs and eight threads per SM, giving 48 threads in total. Imagine the weights as a long row of empty boxes, wrapped into a grid to fit on the page. The first thread fills the first box, the second fills the second box, and so on through all 48 threads. The first thread’s next number then goes into box 49, its next into box 97, and so forth. The black outlines follow this one thread through the grid: the first thread fills every 48th position. The colors identify which processing unit supplies each set of values, while the brightness in the right-hand panel represents the value itself.

Figure 1. How a GPU fills the weights. This simplified example uses six processing units and eight threads per unit, for 48 threads in total. The outlined cells belong to thread 0, which fills every 48th position. Real chips use many more threads, but the placement rule is the same. [Link ↗](https://unemploymentlabs.com/checkpoint-forensics#figure-1)

Now keep the seed fixed, but use a GPU with five SMs instead of six. In our simplified example, that means 40 threads rather than 48. The first thread generates exactly the same sequence, but now puts its numbers in boxes 1, 41, 81, and so on, rather than boxes 1, 49, 97. **Figure 2** follows these numbers as their positions change. Across the grid, only 6 percent of the values match the original arrangement. The seed is right, but the worker count is wrong. **That is what makes the arrangement of model weights a clue to the chip used to create it.**

Figure 2. The same seed on a different GPU. With five processing units and 40 threads in this toy example, thread 0 generates the same sequence but fills every 40th position instead of every 48th. Only 6% of the displayed matrix matches the original arrangement. [Link ↗](https://unemploymentlabs.com/checkpoint-forensics#figure-2)

Reproducing the weights therefore requires two things to be right at once. The seed must generate the right numbers, and the thread count must put them in the right places. A correct seed with the wrong thread count mostly gives the right numbers in the wrong positions; a correct thread count with the wrong seed gives different numbers. **Figure 3** shows why _only the correct combination_ recreates the original arrangement.

Figure 3. Both the seed and the layout must match. The original matrix is reproduced only when the seed and thread count are both correct. Changing either one destroys most of the match. The simplified chips represent a Blackwell B300 and a Hopper H100. Faded cells differ from the published weights. The numbered cells show where thread 0’s numbers land, and the strip beneath each panel shows the numbers themselves

Get started with the Foundation Models framework
The Foundation Models framework is the best way to use any large language model in your app. Whether you’re generating a quick summary or creating dynamic agents, the framework has what you need.
Overview
The Foundation Models framework is a native Swift API for integrating any large language model into your app — including direct access to the Apple Foundation Models on-device and in Private Cloud Compute. Powerful capabilities like guided generation, tool calling, image understanding, and Dynamic Profiles are built in, so you have what you need to build unique experiences.
What’s new in the Foundation Models framework
Meet the Foundation Models framework
Foundation Models framework
Human Interface Guidelines for Generative AI
Image understanding
Multimodal prompts let you pass images alongside text so your app can reason about visual content. This opens up new categories of experiences you can build with image understanding — it's as simple as attaching an image to your prompt. The Vision framework is also integrated directly, giving your model purpose-built tools like OCR for precise text extraction and barcode readers for quick code scanning — all on-device.
What’s new in image understanding
Model support
The Foundation Models framework gives you direct access to the on-device foundation model at the core of Apple Intelligence so you can build experiences that are smart, private, and work without internet connectivity.
On-device models are highly useful for many tasks, yet sometimes you need a larger model for a more complex workflow. The Foundation Models framework now extends to server models — like Claude, Gemini, and more — all through the same Swift API, with full support for features like tool calling and guided generation. , a fundamental component of the framework that allows you to pick the right language model for your app.

Claude
Gemini
Private Cloud Compute
For those just getting started, developers who are enrolled in the App Store Small Business Program and have fewer than two million first-time App Store downloads can access the Apple Foundation Models running on Private Cloud Compute with no cloud API cost.*  This delivers frontier-level intelligence with unparalleled privacy protections, ensuring that your users' data is not stored or accessible to Apple or anyone else.
Learn more about Private Cloud Compute
Build with the new Apple Foundation Model on Private Cloud Compute
Bring an LLM provider to the Foundation Models framework
Dynamic Profiles
Dynamic Profiles are new declarative APIs for continuously updating your session's model, tools, and instructions on the fly. Rather than creating a session with a fixed configuration, you define profiles — each with its own model, temperature, reasoning level, and toolset — and swap between them within a single continuous session. The session transcript is shared across every profile switch, so your app gets more contextual intelligence with less prompting. Dynamic Profiles are designed to be adaptable building blocks: use them to build AI agents, skills, or any other high-level abstraction your app needs.

articles.content:
Title: AI is turning Apple’s app review process into a nightmare for developers

URL Source: https://synthanatomy.com/2026/11/ai-is-turning-apples-app-review-process-into-a-nightmare-for-developers.html

Published Time: 2026-11-12T19:11:01+00:00

Warning: Target URL returned error 400: Bad Request

Markdown Content:
**The surge of AI-generated apps is overwhelming Apple’s app review process, leaving developers caught in the crossfire – two examples among many.**

A flood of new iOS apps has emerged over the last few months. An estimated 10–20 new iOS music apps enter the market every day. This is because AI now makes it possible for anyone to vibe code their own apps and AUv3 plugins.

However, getting an app into the Apple App Store requires going through the app review process. AI has affected not only the number of new releases per day but also Apple’s holy app review process, creating more nightmares than joy for many developers.

### What Is The Apple App Review Process?

Developing and releasing a VST plugin is simple. You set up a website, upload your installers, set a price, and you’re good to go. It’s more complicated on iOS.

To publish an app, you must first join the Apple Developer Program, which costs $99 per year. As a member, you can submit apps with AUv3 support, but they won’t become available immediately.

Whether they are hand-coded or created with the help of AI, all apps must go through Apple’s review process. Every app, whether a synthesizer, effects, game, or utility app, must first get through this barrier.

This process verifies that the app meets requirements, including security standards. That’s a major advantage over many new, freely available VST plugins . You can be confident that everything you download to your iOS or macOS device has been checked and is free of anything suspicious.

So far, the process from submission to release has taken 24 to 48 hours, and sometimes a few days. Developers say the typical review takes a day or two. Apple’s own[App Review guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/distribute/app-review/)state:

> App Review works around the clock, typically reviewing at least 50% of submissions in less than 24 hours and 90% in less than 48 hours.”

### AI And The Impact Of The Apple App Review Process

24-48 days or a few days! That’s what most developers are currently dreaming of. The Apple App Review process is currently on the verge of collapsing due to the flood of new iOS apps (AI or not), or even hallucinating, if you ask iOS developers.

Various developers, including AudioThing, Igor Vasiliev, Sugar Bytes, and others, say their new apps have been stuck in App Review for weeks rather than days, with no updates. As a result, many releases focused on cross-platform compatibility are currently struggling.

Take **Pittsburgh Modular**, for example: their new **Microvolt 3901 synth** was released as a VST on October 27th, while the iOS version only arrived today, November 12th. However, they planned a simultaneous release.

**Igor Vasiliev**‘s new **HollowTone** app (go check out that brilliant app!) also spent weeks stuck in the review process. Most developers can handle a few delays, provided the app is good and ultimately gets purchased.

The problem arises when the app review process becomes erratic—or stops accepting the app altogether—even though it’s just another synth. Some developers have reported this.

### Unfiltered Audio Sinusoidal Run Rhythm

Unfiltered Audio—which offers a range of high-quality AUv3 plugins in the App Store, including the brilliant Battalion drum machine—had trouble bringing its Sinusoidal Run Rhythm to market.

Michael Hetrick of Unfiltered Audio, who’s been in the iOS game for years, wrote on the [Loopy Pro forum](https://forum.loopypro.com/discussion/69387/unfiltered-audio-sinusoidal-run-rhythm-and-srr-midi-public-beta/p2):

> Apple seems to be using AI for automated App Store reviews. SRR got rejected 4 times. The first time, they asked for a video of me demonstrating it (which almost always happens with our plugins).
>
>
> The second time, the editor hallucinated that “Polyharmonic” was an audio technology that we needed to show a documented license for to use the term in the description. The third time, it asked for a video again, this time with the app connected to the “required proprietary hardware”. The fourth time, it flagged SRR MIDI as spam because of its similarity to SRR.
>
>
> It was over a month of back-and-forth, so I threw my hands up and released it audio-only for now. What we will do is bundle the MIDI build into the binary so both AUv3s install.

The app is now available, but only in the audio version. The MIDI version is still not out.

**AudioThing Materia** took 25 days to get approved (1 rejection), and the latest **Seconds**, in collaboration with Hainbach, has been in review for 29 days and counting.

The second case shows that this new Apple app review process AI reality can also cost app developers their livelihoods—especially those who have spent months coding their apps.

### The CRUX Synth Problem

Marek Dendes is a new developer who is currently caught in this precarious situation. He has been working for several months on a flagship Synthesizer called CRUX Synth—a sort of “Serum 2” for iOS.

I’ve been testing the beta for a few weeks now, and it truly is a flagship product. At the moment, it seems the synthesizer won’t be released, as the app has been rejected multiple times by Apple’s App Review process.

He wrote in the [Loopy Pro forum](https://forum.loopypro.com/discussion/69891/crux-build-87-sample-slicer-scale-quantised-modulation-and-much-more):

> My app was REJECTED from submission FOUR TIMES in row. Always same reason (eg. my app is “design spam” and “duplicates existing apps” and it is createed using “app generation template services”) as shown bellow in screenshots. Which is obvious nonsense.
>
>
> I replied on every rejection – no change, again rejected. Obviously nobody reads my explanations. Thing is it goes from “Waiting for Review” into “In Review” and then instantly in second to “Rejected” so this is some automated process and nobody even reads anything i write – so it’s a bit dead end.
>
>
> I submitted multiple appeals to the App Review Board – that did not help, did not get any reply (it’s about 5 days since first appeal submit). Tried also to submit only CRUX without effects to avoid multiple apps submitted at once – same result. There is nothing more i can do.

I reached out to my contacts at Apple, but I didn’t get any real help from them regarding this case.

### My Two Cents (Opinion)

iOS/iPadOS is a fantastic platform for making music on the go. It’s been part of my musical toolkit from the start, and for more than six years, it’s also played an integral role in my hybrid live performance setup.

If you need to submit an app now for release before year’s end, that’s genuinely problematic: you could wait three weeks only to have it rejected. I’m in daily contact with iOS developers.

Many have lost their former euphoria; instead, they express disillusionment and doubt that things will ever be the same. Developers are frustrated by lengthy release delays—and remember, not all submissions are music apps.

With so many new apps launching, even great ones get lost. Do you remember what was published two days ago? This reflects a problem Apple created years ago: ending its affiliate program left media outlets unable to cover iOS meaningfully.

That’s why I’m on [**Patreon.**](https://www.patreon.com/synthanatomy)Today, written coverage of iOS music apps is rare unless they’re backed by major names like Roland, Korg, or Moog.

The iOS market is currently off-kilter—not just because of the flood of AI apps, but also because of Apple itself. Where is the real Apple Intelligence when you actually need it?

If they don’t get a handle on this and start reaching out to iOS developers in person again, as they did early on, I can see the market entering a strange period.

Hey Claude, take me back to the App Store era of 2022. Right now!

**More information here: [Apple](https://developer.apple.com/distribute/app-review/)**

**[iOS News](https://synthanatomy.com/category/music-tech-news/software/ios-software)supported by[Patreon](https://www.patreon.com/synthanatomy)**

articles.content:
Run smarter agents. Use fewer tokens. Our code review bill went up 36x this year. Now a review costs us 18 cents. See how ↓ Quickstart · Case studies · Tour · Templates · Deploy · Docs AgentRun is an open-source platform that supercharges your agents. It adds self-improvement, durable execution and a control plane on top of your favorite agent harness. Your agents become smarter, more fault tolerant and use fewer tokens with every run. An agent's Learning tab: what it kept, and what changed since. Demo data from the console's recorded fixtures. Case studies Code review. Greptile started charging a dollar a review in March, then our agents took off, and our bill went from $180 a month to $6,451. So we built our own reviewer on a cheap model and tuned it on our own PRs. It costs 18 cents a review, and on 30 PRs it had never seen it caught 1.6x the real bugs Greptile did. How we built it · Tune one on your repo Merchant codes. We let Opus figure out how to classify merchants, then handed what it learned to a cheap model. Same job, $0.89 down to $0.12 a merchant. How it works · Do it with your own job Why AgentRun Agents are great at figuring things out. The problem is they figure out the same things over and over. Give an agent a job it has done a hundred times and it rediscovers the same API, rereads the same docs and rebuilds the same plan, and you pay for every token of it. Bring your agent on the harness it runs best on: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode or pi. AgentRun does everything around it: It learns the work. After each run, the agent keeps what will help next time: a note, a skill, or a workflow that does the job without the loop. The next run starts from there. It never loses a run. Every run lives in one store. Kill the server mid-run, start it again, and the run carries on. Give each agent the computer the job needs: a sandbox, a Linux desktop, an Android phone or a browser. You stay in control. Approvals, spend caps and one console for every agent: what needs you, what failed, what's running and what it cost. You don't build the plumbing: provider integrations, recovery, run tracking and learning are all here. Run it on your laptop with one command, in one container, or as a server with runners. Apache-2.0. Start in three steps You need Node 24.22.3 or newer, on macOS or Linux. Start it. npx @parcha/agentrun It starts the server and one runner on port 7340 (or the next free one), keeps everything in ~/.agentrun , and opens the console in your browser. Add one model key. In the console, set a password, then add a key under Settings → Model keys . One OPENROUTER_API_KEY gives every harness a model. An Anthropic key runs pi and Claude Code; an OpenAI key runs pi, Codex and OpenCode. Run your first agent. Open Templates , apply KYB due diligence , and start a run with a company's name and website. It needs nothing but your model key. When it finishes, the run's Report tab has a due diligence report with a verdict and every claim cited. Then open the agent's Learning tab to see what it kept for next time. Rather have your coding agent do it? Tell it: Read agentrun.ai/SKILL.md and set up AgentRun for me . Docker, sandboxes and running it on a server If Docker is running on your machine, new agents get a Docker sandbox with a shell. Its image builds on first use, which takes a few minutes, and the console says when it's ready. Without Docker, agents still read and write files, but get no shell. Want your own server with a URL? Deploy it to Render in one click. Take the tour Workflows that make the call. A step can ask a fast typed question, see how sure the answer is, and pick a route. Here the model leans approve at 0.61, below the workflow's 0.75 bar, so the case goes to review. Every agent in one place. Mission Control opens first: what needs you, what failed, what's running and what it cost, by day, by harness and by tool. Every agent is an API. Start a run from the Playground, then copy the same request into your code. You stay in control. An agent can stop and ask you, and the run waits until you answer. Agents that learn the work Turn it on with "learning": true in an agent's definition. At the end of every run, the agent gets one more turn to say what it would keep. AgentRun checks it, grades it, and commits the keepers to the agent's own git folder. The next run starts from there. flowchart LR start["Run starts from
the agent's main"] --> work["Run does the job"] work --> propose["Last turn proposes
notes, a skill, a workflow"] propose --> check["Code checks,
then one grader"] check -->|kept| commit["Commit to main"] commit --> start Loading Notes are short markdown files, one fact each, in Claude Code's memory format. Skills are how to do a job again, and only a run that finished the job can write one. Learned workflows run as one tool call on any harness, under the run's own cap and tool permissions. Once a learned skill has served 3 runs, the next run is asked for that job as a workflow draft, and a draft is dry-run before it's kept: no model is asked and no tool runs. The agent's Learning tab shows every note, skill and workflow and the log of changes, and each run shows which notes it was given and opened. Retire anything there, or with npx @parcha/agentrun learning retire and the note's ETag. Git keeps the history, so a retired note can come back. What gets kept, and what gets dropped Each agent has a learning folder: plain git with one branch, main . A run reads the index of active notes in its instructions and gets the learned skills beside its own. Code checks every proposal first. An item that breaks a rule of its own (a size or count limit, its name, its shape) is left out and the rest goes on. A secret or a hidden character anywhere in the answer, a file outside the folder, a deletion or a full index drops the whole answer, since no item of it can be trusted. Then one grader judges what it says, and AgentRun commits what passes. A risky rule waits for your OK. A rule the run found in a page or a pasted email, or a note that holds an account number, is dropped. Once an agent's notes outgrow the learning budget, each run gets the ones that bear on its first message, whole, and a line for each of the rest. A run that only ran a learned workflow isn't asked what to keep. Workflows A lot of agents don't need to be agents. Write repeatable work as a typed workflow: tool calls, model steps and fast typed decisions (yes or no, pick one, a score, each with its confidence), with an agent to fall back on when a case is unclear. AgentRun runs it as an agent's revision, under the agent's tool permissions and a cap like any run, and a trigger can start one. An illustration of the control flow in examples/support-answer.mjs , not a recording of a model run. articles.content:
Title: Introducing Edge0-145B: Frontier AI Capabilities on Your Own Computer

URL Source: https://edge0.ai/blog/introducing-edge0-145b-frontier-ai-capabilities-on-your-own-computer

Published Time: 2026-11-12T18:00:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
Today, we're open-sourcing **Edge0-145B and Edge0-120B**, together with our unified inference framework and deployment tools. Edge0-145B is the world's first open-source on-device AI model with 145 billion parameters. It brings coding, reasoning, and agent capabilities that rival frontier cloud models to your own computer.

On-device AI has long forced a tradeoff between model capability and what the hardware can run. Larger models demand more memory, bandwidth, and power; smaller models can struggle with complex work. Moving that work to the cloud adds model-provider fees, data-handling constraints, and a dependence on connectivity.

This release addresses those constraints in four ways:

| **The constraint** | **What Edge0-145B makes possible** |
| --- | --- |
| Large models are difficult to run on personal hardware. | A 145B model runs locally on a compatible laptop, with reported peak memory of 29GB and decoding above 80 tokens/s. |
| Small on-device models can fall short on demanding tasks. | Coding, reasoning, and instruction-following results are competitive with specific frontier cloud models, as the comparisons below show. |
| A useful assistant needs to finish work, not just answer questions. | The model plans, writes and runs code, debugs errors, and checks results visually for projects such as 3D scenes, games, hardware programs, and PCB designs. |
| Cloud workflows bring recurring fees, sensitive-data restrictions, and network dependence. | Local inference incurs no corresponding cloud-model token or API fees; data can stay on the computer, and core capabilities keep working offline. Hardware and electricity still cost money. |

We're releasing the full stack so developers can reproduce the results, evaluate or fine-tune the models, and integrate them into their own products.

Get the [model weights](https://huggingface.co/Edge0), explore the [inference framework](https://github.com/Edge0-AI/Edge0), or try the [Edge0 App](https://github.com/Edge0-AI/Edge0/releases/tag/v0.2.0).

## How We Make 100B+ Parameter AI Run on a Personal Computer

### Edge0-145B Laptop Performance: Memory, Speed, and Power

Edge0-145B makes a 145-billion-parameter model usable on a personal laptop. A useful local model has to fit in memory, process prompts promptly, generate fast enough to use, and keep power consumption under control. It also needs to sustain longer tasks.

| Requirement | Reported Edge0-145B result | What it enables |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Memory | **29GB peak memory** | Runs on a compatible personal laptop, such as a MacBook Pro, without a server. |
| Prompt processing | **1,100+ tokens/s prefill** | Processes long prompts, including dozens of pages of code, before generation begins. |
| Generation | **80+ tokens/s decode** | Generates faster than a person reads. |
| Power | **Approximately 120W typical power** | Sustains operation without throttling in the reported setup. |
| Long tasks | **128K–256K context** | Maintains essentially the same speed on long inputs, supporting extended work. |

Our earlier Edge0-35B phone release reported peak memory below 2.5GB. On an iPhone 18 Pro Max, Edge0-35B delivers 37+ tokens/s using approximately 2.5GB of memory. Edge0-145B has roughly four times as many parameters; its laptop comparison reports 80+ tokens/s and 28GB peak memory. These measurements apply to different models and hardware.

_On-device model scale over time. The chart covers 67 open models of at least 1B parameters from 14 labs, intended for phones, laptops, and AI PCs. Same-size base, instruct, and reasoning variants count once; each line tracks a lab's largest model, including releases before July 2025. Filled points mark new highs and hollow points other releases. The scale is logarithmic below 40B and linear above it. Apple is excluded because its weights are not released. Sources: vendor announcements and model cards._

### Why On-Device Models Have Stayed Small

Memory limits kept most on-device models below 10B parameters before September 2026. Apple Intelligence's on-device foundation model had approximately 3B parameters, while Google's Gemini Nano came in 1.8B and 3.25B versions. Even a 7B model could consume approximately 4GB of memory.

Larger models faced a memory wall. Model weights occupy storage and must be read during generation, competing for limited memory and bandwidth with the operating system and other apps. Even an aggressively compressed 35B model could need approximately 20GB of memory, far more than a phone could make available.

Compute, bandwidth, and power created competing constraints. Larger models offered more capability, but strained memory capacity, generation speed, and battery life. Making models smaller helped them fit, often at the cost of capability.

Privacy alone could not close that gap. Apple Intelligence protected user data, but Apple acknowledged that its on-device model was not designed for agentic applications requiring general world knowledge. The prevailing assumption was that on-device intelligence could not match the cloud.

### Under the Hood of Edge0: Four Layers of Model and Inference Design

We designed Edge0-145B and its inference engine together to reduce the memory and data movement that make large models difficult to run locally. The design spans architecture, training, loading, and scheduling.

**Architecture: share large matrices across sparse experts.** Sharing matrices substantially reduces the weights that must be stored and moved while keeping the expert count unchanged. Each group of 64 experts shares two large matrices, while each expert retains a small set of parameters that captures its differences. Previously, every expert stored a complete set of matrices. Of the model's 145B total parameters, only approximately 10B participate in computation on each inference step.

**Training: build for local execution from day one.** We train the model in its on-device architecture from the outset, with deployment constraints built into its design. This avoids treating local deployment as a compression or pruning step after training a cloud model.

**Loading: pipeline GPU memory, system memory, and SSD access.** Reading and computation overlap across three storage tiers, avoiding serial waits. Frequently used “hot experts” remain in GPU memory. An expert library of approximately 40GB sits in system memory, with experts brought into GPU memory as needed. Approximately 48GB of vocabulary data resides on the SSD and is read on demand.

**Scheduling: use the CPU and GPU together.** The GPU computes cached experts while the CPU handles the remaining work in parallel. Speculative decoding verifies multiple candidate tokens at once, spreading the cost of reading weights across more output tokens. These choices support the reported 80+ tokens/s decode rate.

_Model and inference-engine design work together to make 100B+ parameter inference practical on personal computers. Source: internal testing._

Together, these changes let parameter counts grow from tens of billions to more than a hundred billion without proportional increases in memory use, power consumption, and latency.

## What Edge0 Can Do: Anything From Chat to Complex Work on Your Computer

Edge0-145B can carry a complex task through to a usable result. Its coding and reasoning capabilities support local workflows that combine planning, tool use, execution, debugging, and visual checks. The benchmarks establish its capabilities; the demonstrations show how it puts them to work.

### Coding and reasoning that rival frontier cloud models

Edge0-145B is competitive with specific frontier cloud models across coding, reasoning, knowledge, and instruction following:

*   **Coding:** It scores **64.6 on DeepSWE 1.1**, ahead of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next at 58.7 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 at 54.4.
*   **Reasoning and knowledge:** It scores **90.4 on GPQA-Diamond**, close to DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 at 90.8 and Claude-Opus-4.6 \(Max\) at 91.3.
*   **Instruction following:** It scores **80.6 on IFBench**, ahead of DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 at 79.2 and Claude-Opus-4.6 \(Max\) at 62.5.

Its **86.52 on Terminal-Bench 2.1** also exceeds Qwen3.8-Flash-Next's 83.3, DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731's 82.7, and Claude's 78.2. On AA-LCR, Edge0-145B scores 79.3 to Claude's 78.0. These comparisons apply to the named models and evaluations.

| Model | DeepSWE 1.1 | Terminal-Bench 2.1 | HLE | GPQA-Diamond | IFBench | AA-LCR |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Edge0-145B** | **64.6** | **86.52** | **35.4** | **90.4** | **80.6** | **79.3** |
| Edge0-120B | 53.6 | 81.3 | 31.0 | 87.4 | 79.3 | 81.0 |
| Qwen3.8-Flash-Next | 58.7 | 83.3 | 35.9 | 91.7 | 81.3 | 79.1 |
| Qwen3.8-27B | 42.2 | 73.0 | 30.8 | 89.2 | 79.5 | 82.0 |
| DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 | 54.4 | 82.7 | 33.8 | 90.8 | 79.2 | 79.7 |
| Flint 40B | — | 54.9 | — | — | 89.2 | — |
| Muse Glimmer | — | 51.7 | 22.0 | 83.5 | 77.0 | 83.3 |
| Gemma 4 | — | 43.4 | 22.7 | 85.7 | 76.0 | 62.0 |
| Claude-Opus-4.6 \(Max\) | — | 78.2 | 40.0 | 91.3 | 62.5 | 78.0 |

_Scores are percentages; higher is better. A dash means no public score is available, rather than a score of zero._

Edge0, Qwen, DeepSeek, and Claude results come from Edge0's internal evaluations. Claude-Opus-4.6 has no public DeepSWE 1.1 score. For Flint, Muse Glimmer, and Gemma 4, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and IFBench results come from the Recursive Flint evaluation; HLE, GPQA, and AA-LCR results come from Artificial Analysis.

The largest gains over Qwen3.8-27B, a mainstream on-device model baseline, are in agent and coding work: **18.5% on Terminal-Bench and 53.1% on DeepSWE**. The relative gains on HLE, GPQA, and IFBench are 14.9%, 1.3%, and 1.4%, respectively.

DeepSWE 1.1 and Terminal-Bench 2.1 evaluate agent and coding work. HLE, GPQA-Diamond, and IFBench cover reasoning, knowledge, and instruction following. The complete evaluation setup, hardware environment, and reproduction instructions are being released with our technical report.

### Competitive capability with a smaller memory footprint

Edge0-145B combines a **72.8 mean score across six benchmarks with 29GB measured peak memory**. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next averages 71.7, with an estimated 70GB footprint for standard 4-bit deployment. That puts Edge0-145B at about 40% of the estimated baseline memory while delivering comparable or higher capability, enabling local use on a 48GB laptop.

| Model | Mean across six benchmarks | Memory footprint \(measured or estimated\) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Edge0-145B** | **72.8** | **29GB** |
| Edge0-120B | 68.9 | 29GB |
| Qwen3.8-27B | 66.1 | Approximately 18GB* |
| Qwen3.8-Flash-Next | 71.7 | Approximately 70GB* |
| DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 | 70.1 | Approximately 87GB* |

The means cover DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal-Bench 2.1, HLE, GPQA-Diamond, IFBench, and AA-LCR. Edge0 memory figures are measured internal peaks. Asterisked baseline figures are estimates for standard 4-bit deployment and remain to be measured. Claude is excluded because it is cloud-only and has no DeepSWE score.

[Figure: Quality versus peak memory, with 48GB laptop and 64GB workstation capacities marked. Lower memory and higher scores are better; the chart's vertical axis does not start at zero.]

### Local agents that plan, code, run, and check their work

A single natural-language request can start an entire local workflow. Edge0-145B breaks down the requirements, plans the steps, writes code, and calls tools to run it. When something fails, it debugs and repairs the code. It then takes screenshots to inspect the result and keeps iterating until the work is complete.
